name: World Languages: More Practice, Human Judgment
title: World Languages: More Practice, Human Judgment
answer: AI can give world language students far more practice than a single class period allows, through conversation partners, writing feedback, and pronunciation tools. The evidence is strongest for writing feedback and weakest for conversation practice, so schools should pilot rather than adopt wholesale. The teacher's judgment, especially their ear for pronunciation and their control of grades, stays central.

crumbs.name: Social Studies, Civics, and World Languages

sections.body: Learning a language demands a great deal of practice, and finding enough practice partners is hard. AI can help close that gap by offering drills in many languages, with automatic protections for younger users, and by letting school configured voice tools hold simple conversations matched to a student's level. This gives students much more speaking time than a normal class period can provide. The idea solves the problem of scarce practice partners and limited classroom minutes. It does not replace the teacher, it adds repetitions that students would otherwise not get.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the classroom, the tools take different forms depending on the skill. For speaking, school configured voice tools can hold simple conversations at the student's level, which is most useful where a class period cannot give each student enough talk time. For writing, students write in the target language and receive AI feedback, then revise, with the design from Chapter 6 applied so that revision is required and the teacher keeps the grade. For pronunciation, speech tools flag sounds a student is producing incorrectly, and detailed feedback on specific sounds appears to help more than general comments. The text does not give separate grade bands beyond noting that Duolingo carries automatic protections for users under 13 and that tenth graders took part in the writing trial.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels the evidence for conversation partners as still thin. A small case study of six adult learners found that a voice assistant understood more than 80 percent of their commands while they practiced Japanese on their own (Dizon et al., 2022), which the text calls encouraging but limited because it involved adults and a very small group, so schools should treat conversation practice as a promising idea to pilot rather than a proven method. Writing feedback in the target language has stronger support: in a randomized trial, tenth graders writing in English as a foreign language revised better and felt more motivated after receiving AI feedback (Meyer et al., 2023). A review of AI writing tools in university language classes found mixed results, often from studies tied to the companies that made the tools and rarely with comparison groups (Alharbi, 2023). Pronunciation feedback is described as useful but limited, with detailed feedback on specific sounds appearing to help more than general comments (Bashori et al., 2024), while speech recognition trained mostly on adult native speakers can struggle with young learners and may smooth over the very errors a student needs to fix (Michot et al., 2024).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits. Conversation practice should be piloted, not treated as proven, because the supporting study was small and involved adults. Writing feedback tools carry a risk of mixed results, and the review found many studies were tied to the companies that made the tools and rarely used comparison groups, so the feedback design from Chapter 6 applies, with required revision and the grade kept by the teacher. Pronunciation tools can miss or smooth over errors, particularly for young learners, because speech recognition is trained mostly on adult native speakers, so the teacher's ear remains essential. Across all three uses, the decisions that stay with a person are the teacher's judgment of student work and the grade itself.
